chunks: Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, from al-Faḍl ibn Shādhān and ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, all together from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥafṣ ibn al-Bakhtarī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

Indeed, Jibrāʾīl عليه السلام dug five rivers with his foot, and the tongue of the water followed him: the Euphrates, the Tigris, the Nile of Egypt, Mihrān, and the river of Balkh. So whatever they water, or whatever is watered from them, belongs to the Imam, and the sea surrounding the world belongs to the Imam.

key_terms.الْإِمَامِ: the Imam, to whom these watered domains are said to belong
key_terms.جَبْرَئِيلَ: Jibrāʾīl عليه السلام, the angel mentioned as the one who dug the rivers
key_terms.خَمْسَةَ أَنْهَارٍ: five rivers specifically named in the narration
key_terms.لِسَانُ الْمَاءِ: the flow or leading extension of the water that followed

ai.seo_question: How does al-Kāfī describe the Imam’s authority over major rivers and the seas of the world?
ai.summary: This hadith attributes the emergence of five major rivers to Jibrāʾīl عليه السلام and states that what is irrigated by them belongs to the Imam. It also affirms that the sea encompassing the world is for the Imam, expressing the Imam’s divinely designated authority over the earth’s major natural domains and resources.
